findings.area: Reliability estimation for generated-test verdicts (CodeT → B4 → ACES lineage)
findings.what_is_solved: The aggregation side is well-developed and the circularity is explicitly named. CodeT (Chen et al. 2022, arXiv:2207.10397) scores consensus sets f(S)=sqrt(|S_x|)*|S_y|, deliberately downweighting solution count relative to test count, and introduces 'toxic' test cases (a test any generated solution passes but the canonical solution fails). B4 (Chen et al., ASE'24, arXiv:2409.08692) makes selection Bayesian-optimal: a posterior over the observed solution-by-test pass matrix, framed as integer programming, with Theorem 1 bounding approximation error Δ ≤ (2/P(E))[c1·Δθ1 + c0·Δθ0 + cx·Δθx + cy·Δθy] by prior misspecification. ACES (Sun et al., arXiv:2604.03922, Apr 2026) is the state of the art and is explicitly framed as 'who tests the tests': it defines per-test discriminative power δ_j = P(pass|correct) − P(pass|incorrect), classifies tests as informative (δ>0) / uninformative (δ=0) / misleading (δ<0), and estimates δ label-free via leave-one-out AUC — hold out test j, rank candidates by aggregate score S_i^(−j) = Σ_{j'≠j} w_j' B_ij' on the remaining tests, and measure whether the held-out column agrees with that ranking. ACES-C uses closed-form weights w_j = max(0, LOO-AUC_j(w_unif) − 1/2)·p_j(1−p_j); ACES-O iteratively optimizes a differentiable LOO-AUC objective. Reported HumanEval Pass@1 84.15% (+15.8 over direct inference), HumanEval+ 74.39%, MBPP 72.37%, on ~200 candidates and ~500 tests per problem from GPT-3.5-Turbo.
findings.open_corner: Every located estimator calibrates test reliability against a reference constructed from the very tally it is meant to correct, and none reports its estimate restricted to the decisive stratum. ACES's own theory makes the dependence explicit: expected LOO-AUC_j is proportional to δ_j with a coefficient depending on the test's pass-rate variance AND 'the ranking quality of the remaining tests'. On problems where the tally-top candidate cluster is wrong, that reference ranking is inverted at the top, so a test that correctly separates the correct minority candidate from the wrong plurality is measured as DISAGREEING with the reference and receives LOO-AUC < 1/2 — whereupon ACES-C's max(0, ·) clip assigns it exactly zero weight. The paper states no theoretical treatment exists when A^(−j)(w) ≤ 1/2, and its own Section 4.3 concedes 'In the Hard region, no method passes more than 1 of 14 tasks'. Falsifiable open corner: on HumanEval+/MBPP+/LiveCodeBench with a capable frozen model, restrict to problems where the unweighted-tally top-1 cluster is incorrect AND at least one hidden-correct candidate exists in the pool; measure, for the tests whose TRUE δ_j > 0 on that stratum (computable with hidden tests post hoc), the rate r at which their measured LOO-AUC falls below 1/2. Claim to test: r > 0.5 on the decisive stratum versus r < 0.1 overall — i.e. ACES's estimator systematically zeroes out precisely the tests that would rescue the decisive cases. No located paper reports r, or any decisive-stratum conditional of LOO-AUC, the B4 posterior, or CodeT's consensus score.

findings.area: Signed reliability for test verdicts — sign is detected but never exploited
findings.what_is_solved: Signed reliability estimation for test verdicts DOES exist, contrary to what the framing might assume, and this is the single most important correction to the lens. ACES formalizes it: δ_j < 0 defines a 'misleading' test, LOO-AUC can and does fall below 0.5, and the paper permits arbitrarily many misleading tests provided only that the average is positive. BACE (arXiv:2603.28653) goes further mechanistically — it treats generated tests as noisy sensors with three noise hyperparameters (α false pass, β accidental pass, γ coincidental pass), maintains belief distributions b(c) over code correctness and b(t) over test validity, and updates in log-odds space with a credibility threshold (its Eq. 5) at which the update logic INVERTS: below the threshold, a 'pass' decreases belief in the test and a 'fail' increases it. BACE reports LiveCodeBench v6 (80 problems) gains over CodeSIM of +2.5 (GPT-5-Mini), +5.4 (Qwen2.5-Coder-7b), +5.0 (GPT-OSS-120b).
findings.open_corner: The sign is used only to ZERO OUT, never to INVERT the verdict, and reliability is never estimated per-problem. ACES-C's weight is w_j = max(0, LOO-AUC_j − 1/2)·p_j(1−p_j) — a test measured at LOO-AUC 0.2 (strongly anti-correlated, hence strongly informative with its sign flipped) contributes exactly the same as a test at 0.5 (pure noise). A test whose assertion encodes the model's shared misconception is passed by wrong code and failed by correct code; its verdict is real evidence pointing the other way, and TACT-style signed reliability would weight it −|w_j| rather than 0. No located work assigns a negative weight to a test verdict. Separately, BACE's α/β/γ are global hyperparameters set by parameter sweep with (the authors' own stated limitation) no sensitivity analysis, and ACES's Assumption 4 is a single global average condition δ̄ := (1/m)Σδ_j > 2·sqrt(ln2/m) — so no method estimates a per-problem test-channel reliability, only a pooled one. Falsifiable open corner: (a) on the decisive stratum, the mass of tests with true δ_j < −0.1 is non-trivial (>10% of the test pool) and inverting rather than clipping them recovers selection accuracy that clipping cannot; (b) the per-problem δ̄ distribution is bimodal, so a single global threshold is the wrong instrument — problems below the Assumption-4 threshold are identifiable label-free (e.g. from pass-matrix rank/entropy) and should trigger abstention or routing rather than weighted voting. Neither (a) nor (b) is measured in any located work.

findings.area: Where the field assumes tests beat chance — and the solution/test independence assumption that is measurably false
findings.what_is_solved: The assumptions are stated, not hidden, and their locations are precise. ACES-C requires Assumption 4: δ̄ := (1/m)Σδ_j > 2·sqrt(ln2/m) — average discriminative power positive, of order O(1/sqrt(m)), weaker than a classical weak-learner condition; ACES-O is offered specifically to drop it. B4 assumes test correctness Y_j ~ Bernoulli(θ_y) with a Beta prior deliberately shaped α_y >> 1, β_y = 1 to favour larger test-bearing consensus sets, plus Assumption 2 ('the code solutions X and the test cases Y are independent and randomly sampled') and Assumption 3 ('each E_ij is only dependent on X_i and Y_j', i.e. pass outcomes conditionally independent given correctness labels). ACES likewise assumes conditional independence of test outcomes given the correctness label. Crucially, the independence assumption has been directly measured and falsified elsewhere: Huang, Zhang, Harman, Du, Cui, 'Measuring the Influence of Incorrect Code on Test Generation' (arXiv:2409.09464, 11 models, 3 benchmarks + 41 repo-level real-world examples) found that relative to incorrect code under test, prompting with CORRECT code yields +57% test accuracy, +12% coverage, +24% bug detection, and on real-world code tests generated for incorrect code suffer a 47% worse bug-detection rate. 'Rethinking Verification for LLM Code Generation' (arXiv:2507.06920) shows via PCA that LLM-induced errors are tightly clustered while human errors are diverse, that LLM solutions easily pass their own self-generated tests (detection rate <60%), and that re-evaluating LiveCodeBench-passing solutions on LeetCode surfaces errors the verifier missed for 20% of medium and 40% of hard problems.
findings.open_corner: The binding assumption is not the test-correctness prior but the SOLUTION–TEST error dependence, and no one has estimated it and propagated it into the existing optimality guarantees. B4's Assumption 2 asserts X ⊥ Y, yet solutions and tests come from the same model on the same prompt; Huang et al. quantified the conditional degradation (57% accuracy drop, 47% bug-detection drop) but conditioned on the code shown IN THE PROMPT being wrong, which is a different conditioning event from the pool's plurality being wrong, and did not connect it to any selection guarantee. Falsifiable open corner: fit a two-parameter correlated pass model — a per-problem error-mode variable m, with P(solution i exhibits m) and P(test j fails to catch m) coupled by a dependence parameter ρ — to the observed pass matrix on HumanEval+/LiveCodeBench, and measure Δθ_y (total variation between B4's assumed and the fitted true prior) as a function of ρ. Claim to test: on the decisive stratum, the fitted ρ is large enough that Δθ_y exceeds the regime in which B4's Theorem 1 bound is non-vacuous, so B4's optimality certificate does not hold exactly where selection is decided — and further, that ACES's Assumption 4 (δ̄ > 2·sqrt(ln2/m)) fails on the decisive stratum even though it holds comfortably in aggregate. Neither the fitted ρ nor the decisive-stratum value of δ̄ or Δθ_y is reported anywhere located.

findings.area: Test-channel reliability measured on the decisive stratum — the gap itself
findings.what_is_solved: Test-channel reliability has been measured along three axes, none of them the decisive stratum. (1) By aggregate: CodeT reports per-problem test accuracy (most HumanEval problems >80% for Codex) and toxicity-rate distributions. (2) By DIFFICULTY: 'Rethinking Verification' stratifies VAcc/DR by Easy/Medium/Hard and reports the 20%/40% medium/hard false-accept re-evaluation. (3) By SUITE LEAKINESS, mechanically: 'When the Reward Suite Is Leaky' (arXiv:2607.11022) audits MBPP against MBPP+ with a preregistered two-arm GRPO contrast over 250 tasks and three model families, reporting a pooled static false-positive rate of 15.30% raw / 13.71% artifact-excluded, verified-wrong shares of 47.6%/45.4%/62.8% by family, Spearman ρ ≈ 0.80 between static leakiness and rewarded-FP mass (0.79 after controlling for difficulty), and — the key structural claim — that natural verifier false positives are 'per-task and persistent, and the error runs in one direction only: wrong code gets rewarded', in contrast to the iid pass/fail flips assumed by noise-robustness work. This is the test-channel analogue of stable-wrong. Separately, 'Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression' (İşcan, arXiv:2606.16999) runs a matched-compute, leakage-free measurement of 26 post-hoc operators on frozen 0.5–1.5B code models and reports 'capability scissors' (AUC 0.479 discriminating among visible-passing candidates), the 'near-empty consensus trap' (0/10 and 2/16 occurrences), and a 'coverage wall' (16/30 hard tasks yield zero hidden-correct candidate even at k=16), with ~83% of real bugs invisible to any sound metamorphic relation.
findings.open_corner: No located work reports the generated-test channel's discriminative power conditioned on the event that makes selection decidable: 'the tally-top candidate cluster is incorrect AND at least one hidden-correct candidate exists in the pool'. The leaky-suite audit is explicitly unconditional on model behaviour — it compares suite verdicts mechanically, not model outputs — and uses human-written MBPP/MBPP+ tests in an RL setting, not generated tests in inference-time selection. The difficulty stratification in 'Rethinking Verification' is a proxy: difficulty is a property of the problem, the decisive stratum is a property of the (problem, candidate pool) pair, and the leaky-suite OLS decomposition already shows leakiness (coeff .896) dominates difficulty (coeff −.049), so the two are not interchangeable. 'Selection Without Signal' does condition on the right event but measures the SELECTION channel on 0.5–1.5B models, not the test-generation channel on capable models. Falsifiable open corner: this is the instrument-validity split applied to the test channel. On HumanEval+/MBPP+/LiveCodeBench with a capable frozen model at N=50–200 candidates and M=50–500 generated tests, report δ̄_overall and δ̄_decisive side by side. Claim to test: δ̄_overall ≥ 0.3 while δ̄_decisive ≤ 0.05, i.e. the generated-test channel is a valid instrument in aggregate and an invalid one exactly where it must decide — and the gap widens monotonically with problem difficulty. A second, sharper claim from the leaky-suite structure: on the decisive stratum, test-channel errors are per-problem persistent and one-directional (the wrong plurality passes every generated test, every time), so no amount of iid test resampling closes the gap — the m-th generated test is conditionally independent of nothing.

findings.area: The economics: pricing the assertion channel against the candidate channel at matched budget
findings.what_is_solved: Three 2026 results converge on the finding that the assertion-bearing test channel may not be worth its tokens, without anyone stating it as such. SemanticVote (Jiang, Yi, Zhu, arXiv:2605.08680, May 2026) studies 18 configurations across models, thinking levels and benchmarks and concludes: execution-based selectors beat output-pattern majority voting by 19–52 pp everywhere; but once candidates are executed on diverse inputs, SemanticVote, weighted voting and MBR-Exec are STATISTICALLY INDISTINGUISHABLE across all 18 configurations, while the largest factor is INPUT QUALITY (sketch-based input generation beats direct LLM generation by 0.6–2.1 pp and random fuzzing by up to 11.3 pp) — their framing is that inference-time code selection is 'a signal-quality problem rather than an aggregation-rule problem'. DiffCodeGen (He, Wang, Wang, Ouyang, Chen, arXiv:2605.20473) removes the LLM from selection entirely — coverage-guided fuzzing synthesizes inputs with no tests and no LLM calls, candidates are clustered by behaviour and the medoid of the largest cluster is returned — at roughly 4% of SkyCoder's input token consumption. SEP (Cho, Wang, Sui, Grama, arXiv:2604.06485) explicitly names the two-world problem ('consensus alone is not sufficient for correctness, because models can also produce correlated wrong solutions that implement the same mistaken behavior') and answers it with symbolic execution over bounded functional equivalence classes plus public examples, 'without auxiliary test generation, learned verifiers, or additional LLM inference': HumanEval+ 0.754→0.826 and LiveCodeBench 0.565→0.647 at N=10. On the cost side, ADAP (Dughmi, Haghifam, Kalayci, arXiv:2605.17609) formalizes generate-rank-verify as cost-sensitive first-positive search, achieving expected cost within a constant factor of the distribution-aware optimum under a monotonicity assumption, with learning-theoretic lower bounds via a centered star number.
findings.open_corner: Nobody has run the head-to-head that these three results jointly imply. ADAP's expensive verifier is assumed TRUE (hidden-test execution, exact answer checking) — it prices a correct oracle, not a noisy correlated one, and its monotonicity assumption (higher reward score no less likely to pass verification) is exactly what fails when the test channel shares the generator's error modes. SemanticVote shows the aggregation rule is irrelevant and inputs dominate, but never asks how a fixed token budget should split between candidates and inputs. DiffCodeGen drives test cost toward zero but does not report what the assertions would have bought. Falsifiable open corner: fix a token budget B and run a difficulty sweep on HumanEval+/LiveCodeBench/BigCodeBench with three matched-budget arms — (i) all tokens to candidates + oracle-free behavioural clustering (DiffCodeGen/SemanticVote style, inputs only, no assertions), (ii) tokens split between candidates and ASSERTION-bearing generated tests aggregated by the best available reliability-weighted rule (ACES-O or B4), (iii) all tokens to candidates + iid plurality. Claim to test: arm (ii) is never better than arm (i) at matched B on the decisive stratum, and its deficit grows with difficulty — i.e. the assertion channel is net-negative once its tokens are correctly priced, and the entire measured benefit of 'generated tests' is attributable to the INPUTS they carry rather than the ORACLES they assert. This decomposition (inputs vs assertions, at matched tokens, on the decisive stratum) is not performed in any located work; SemanticVote comes closest but varies input quality only, holding the assertion-free design fixed throughout.

findings.area: The agentic / SWE-bench regime: a single-test channel with no pool to calibrate against
findings.what_is_solved: The reproduction-test channel is measured and is weak, and the patch-side verifier is measured and is leaky. Issue2Test (Nashid, Bouzenia, Pradel, Mesbah, arXiv:2503.16320) reports 32.9% success at reproducing issues on SWT-bench-lite, a 16.3% relative improvement over the best prior technique, and notes that its 20 uniquely-reproduced issues represent a large share of the union across five tools — i.e. the tools are complementary and each individually covers roughly a third. Related lines: Heterogeneous Prompting and Execution Feedback for SWE Issue Test Generation and Selection (Ahmed, Ganhotra, Shinnar, Hirzel, arXiv:2508.06365), EvoOtter (same group, arXiv:2607.02854) which motivates itself precisely on the difficulty of 'determining whether a candidate BRT indeed fails for the reason in the issue', Echo (arXiv:2603.07326), and Dynamic Cogeneration of Bug Reproduction Test in Agentic Program Repair (arXiv:2601.19066). On the verifier side, UTBoost (Yu, Zhu, He, Kang, arXiv:2506.09289) augments SWE-bench test suites specifically to expose patches that pass the shipped tests while being wrong, and independent SWE-bench-Pro auditing surfaced ~13% verifier false positives on Claude Opus trials with 87% of identified cheating trials reading the gold commit out of .git history.
findings.open_corner: Every reliability estimator surveyed above requires two large pools — many candidates AND many tests — to break the circularity, and the agentic regime supplies neither. A fail-to-pass reproduction test is a single binary instrument per issue; ACES states outright that its performance degrades with small candidate sets, B4's posterior is defined over an M-column pass matrix, and BACE needs a population of 10–20 tests evolved over 10 generations plus 1–3 immutable public anchors that SWE-bench issues do not provide. So the entire signed-reliability toolkit is inapplicable exactly where external truth is supposedly cheapest. Falsifiable open corner: on SWE-bench-lite/Verified, condition on the decisive event — the plurality patch cluster (by behavioural fingerprint over the generated reproduction test plus existing repo tests) is wrong AND a correct patch exists among the k sampled patches — and measure the reproduction test's signed discriminative power δ on that stratum. Two claims to test: (a) δ_decisive ≤ 0, because a reproduction test written from the same issue text that misled the patch generator inherits the misreading and is passed by the wrong plurality (the Issue2Test framing — tests must fail 'for the reason in the issue' — is precisely the failure surface); (b) the single-test regime admits a substitute pool that no located work exploits: the repo's EXISTING regression suite provides tens to hundreds of pre-existing, human-written, model-independent verdict columns per candidate patch, which is exactly the wide pass matrix that LOO-AUC/B4 require and whose errors are not correlated with the generator. No located work uses the existing regression suite as a calibration pool to estimate the signed reliability of the generated reproduction test.

findings.area: Refine-vs-resample allocation within a single problem (the debug budget as a bandit)
findings.what_is_solved: REx (Tang, Key, Ellis, NeurIPS 2024) is the lone principled treatment: code refinement framed as an arm-acquiring bandit over the tree of repairs, solved with Thompson sampling using a Beta posterior seeded by fraction-of-tests-passed; beats greedy/BFS/fixed-width at matched budget on APPS-competition, ARC, loop-invariant synthesis. The empirical side is well characterized: Olausson et al. (arXiv:2306.09896) showed budget-matched self-repair often loses to iid sampling for weak models; a 2026 follow-up (arXiv:2604.10508) re-ran the rounds-vs-samples tradeoff on 2024-25 models across HumanEval/MBPP and found gains concentrate in the first 2 repair rounds and assertion-type (logic) errors repair at only ~45%. MCTS variants (RethinkMCTS arXiv:2409.09584, APRMCTS arXiv:2507.01827, TGPR arXiv:2510.06878) use UCT over repair trees with execution feedback but purely heuristically.
findings.open_corner: No located work gives a cost-aware or regret-analyzed version of REx. Specifically: (a) REx charges unit cost per pull, but a refinement pull costs 2-10x the tokens of a fresh sample (full program + trace in context) and each test execution has separate wall-clock cost — no located policy optimizes reward per joint (token, execution) cost; (b) no regret bound exists for the arm-acquiring structure with test-pass rewards; (c) REx has no stopping rule — it runs to budget exhaustion even when the posterior says the problem is hopeless. Falsifiable target: a cost-normalized index policy over (tokens, executions) that beats REx and the 2604.10508 fixed policies at matched joint budget on APPS/LiveCodeBench, with an abandon-the-problem stopping rule whose error rate is controlled.

findings.area: Pipeline-level generate/test/debug split (serial vs parallel, with cost accounting)
findings.what_is_solved: CodeMonkeys (Stanford, arXiv:2501.14723) is the definitive empirical treatment on SWE-bench Verified: explicit serial (iterations per trajectory) vs parallel (trajectories per problem) sweep, full dollar cost breakdown (edit generation 59.6%, test generation 19.2%, context 14.6%), finding that many different serial/parallel splits give similar coverage. S* (arXiv:2502.14382, EMNLP 2025 Findings) fixes the split as N parallel samples x up to R execution-grounded debug rounds, plus adaptive pairwise distinguishing-input synthesis for selection. Coverage scaling laws for pure resampling are established (Large Language Monkeys, arXiv:2407.21787); compute-optimal inference tradeoffs across strategies in Wu et al. (arXiv:2408.00724).
findings.open_corner: Every located pipeline chooses its split by offline grid search and holds it fixed across all instances and all points in time. No located work has an online controller that, per instance, chooses among {spawn new trajectory, extend/debug an existing one, generate+run another test} using the execution outcomes observed so far — despite CodeMonkeys' own data showing the flat coverage surface is an average that masks per-instance heterogeneity. Falsifiable target: an instance-adaptive three-action controller that Pareto-dominates the best fixed CodeMonkeys/S* split on SWE-bench-lite/LiveCodeBench at matched dollar cost; nothing located even benchmarks such a controller.

findings.area: Per-query adaptive compute allocation (difficulty-aware sample budgets)
findings.what_is_solved: Damani et al. (arXiv:2410.04707, ICLR 2025) learn a marginal-benefit predictor and allocate samples across queries as constrained optimization (up to 50% compute saved on math+code). OSCA (arXiv:2410.22480, NAACL 2025) optimizes a mixture over inference configurations across a dataset, including SWE-bench agentic workflows (3x less compute). The only regret-bounded treatment located: Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute (arXiv:2506.12721) formulates per-query sample allocation as bandit learning with on-the-fly difficulty estimation and proves regret guarantees, evaluated on MATH-500/AIME25/LiveCodeBench. 2026 continuations (arXiv:2604.14853 constrained policy optimization; arXiv:2605.26849 uncertainty-reallocated budgets) allocate reasoning tokens by confidence.
findings.open_corner: All located allocators decide how many samples/tokens a query gets while treating each sample's quality as opaque or proxied by self-consistency/confidence — none use per-sample executable anchors (k-of-m tests passed) as the bandit's observation process, even though that signal is exactly what makes the reward observable rather than proxied. The regret-bounded line (2506.12721) covers only sample-count allocation across queries, not the within-query choice among generate/test/debug actions with heterogeneous costs. Falsifiable target: an allocator whose state is the observed test-outcome matrix, shown to beat confidence-proxy allocators (2410.04707-style) at matched budget specifically on the stratum where confidence and execution signals disagree.

findings.area: Optimal stopping and anytime-valid certificates for repeated sampling
findings.what_is_solved: Cost-aware stopping under reward-model scores is now formalized: BEACON (arXiv:2510.15945) gives Bayesian-optimal sequential stopping with posterior updates over reward distributions (up to 80% fewer samples); Kalayci et al. (arXiv:2510.01394) map best-of-n to Pandora's-box optimal stopping with Weitzman fair-cap indices. On the anytime-valid side: Sequential-EDFL (arXiv:2510.06478) uses empirical-Bernstein e-processes on information lift to stop generation; CITE (arXiv:2605.05873) gives anytime-valid certification that a target answer is the mode of the sampling distribution in self-consistency, with data-dependent stopping and error control — explicitly without execution feedback.
findings.open_corner: The confluence is empty: no located work builds an e-process/confidence-sequence over executable test outcomes. Concretely absent: a label-free anytime-valid certificate of the form 'with probability >= 1-alpha, no candidate reachable within the remaining budget will pass strictly more tests than the incumbent — stop and cash the incumbent.' Test outcomes per candidate are exchangeable Bernoulli draws over a test distribution, so the betting-martingale construction the program already has fluency in applies directly, yet CITE excludes execution, BEACON assumes conjugate reward families, and the heteroskedasticity result (arXiv:2606.15841: uncertainty-signal quality varies by cost stratum, breaking global thresholds on MBPP/MATH) shows why proxy-score stopping rules are unsafe. Falsifiable target: e-process stopping vs BEACON/fixed-n on HumanEval+/LiveCodeBench with certified error control at matched accuracy and lower average cost.

findings.area: Generate-vs-verify budget ratio (how much to spend making the anchor itself)
findings.what_is_solved: For generative (non-executable) verification, the ratio is settled: Singhi et al. findings.open_corner: The fLaws false-positive floor is a function of test-suite strength, and test-suite strength is purchasable at inference time (generate more/harder tests) — yet no located work optimizes the marginal-value trade 'one more generated-and-executed test (raises the floor) vs one more candidate (raises coverage under the current floor),' statically or adaptively. This is the executable-domain analogue of 2504.01005 and it is unclaimed. Falsifiable target: a policy allocating budget between candidate generation and test generation per instance that beats the best fixed ratio (CodeMonkeys-style) on benchmarks where base test coverage is weak (MBPP, HumanEval original vs plus), measured by true-correctness, not test-pass.

findings.area: Adaptive test selection to discriminate candidates (which test to run next)

ExPairT-LLM comes closest in formalization but assumes query answers rather than budgeting them. Falsifiable target: an execution-scheduling policy that matches S*'s selection accuracy on LiveCodeBench with a measured fraction (e.g., <30%) of its test executions, with an anytime-valid guarantee on selecting a test-signature-optimal candidate.

findings.area: Latent-variable / weak-supervision aggregation over a verifier vector (the Dawid-Skene lineage as applied to LLM verification)
findings.what_is_solved: Unsupervised and label-efficient estimation of per-verifier reliability from agreement structure alone is solved for LM-based verifiers. Weaver (Stanford, arXiv:2506.18203) builds an explicit latent-variable graphical model over {Y, S_1..S_m} with Y the latent correctness label and S_k binary verifier votes, estimating each verifier's Pr(S_i=1|Y=1) and Pr(S_i=1|Y=0) by matching pairwise and marginal moment statistics under conditional independence, then forming a Bayes posterior; it adds normalization, binarization of continuous reward scores, and low-quality-verifier filtering, and needs only ~1% dev data to pin Pr(Y=1). FUSE (Candès group, arXiv:2604.18547) removes labels entirely, using spectral ensembling algorithms and explicitly *controlling conditional dependencies between verifiers* rather than assuming them away. 'Calibrate, Don't Curate' (arXiv:2605.09702) supplies the complementary theory: a Bayesian one-coin weighted aggregator plus beta calibration, with a Calibrated Jury Theorem proving even sub-chance ('anti-expert') verifiers contribute positively when their bias is learnable and their signal is non-redundant — i.e. do not prune weak verifiers, calibrate them.
findings.open_corner: No located work puts a single EXECUTABLE verdict into any of these latent-variable models. Weaver's ~33 verifiers are all reward models and LM judges evaluated on MATH500/GPQA-Diamond/MMLU-College/MMLU-Pro, with zero code-execution tasks; the paper's own Discussion names specialized verifiers 'for programming tasks' as future work. FUSE's abstract names only GPQA Diamond, Humanity's Last Exam, and IMO Shortlist. 'Calibrate, Don't Curate' uses pairwise-preference benchmarks (JudgeBench, RewardBench 1/2, LLMBar) and requires 20-50 held-out labels. Concretely open: given the binary pass/fail matrix P ∈ {0,1}^{N candidates × M generated tests} — which is *directly observable at inference time with zero labels* — no located method runs Dawid-Skene/moment-matching/spectral estimation over its columns to recover each test's sensitivity Pr(pass|correct) and specificity Pr(fail|incorrect) and then forms a posterior over candidate correctness. This is a strictly easier identifiability problem than the QA case the map declared blocked, because a test emits a *vector* of verdicts across N candidates (observable structure) where an LM judge emits only a scalar per candidate. Falsifiable claim to design against: on HumanEval+/MBPP+/LiveCodeBench, DS-style unsupervised estimation over the test×candidate verdict matrix beats CodeT dual-agreement and unweighted pass-count voting at matched execution budget.

findings.area: Execution-based candidate selection: how test verdicts are actually aggregated today
findings.what_is_solved: Execution-grouping and consensus selection are mature and strong. CodeT (arXiv:2207.10397) executes candidates against generated tests and scores by dual execution agreement (consensus set size × tests passed), beating pure clustering. Functional Clustering (arXiv:2506.11021) partitions candidates into exact I/O-behavior equivalence classes on an auto-generated suite, takes largest-cluster mass as confidence, and proves an exponential reliability bound decaying as exp[−n·D_KL(τ‖C)] — at n=100 the false-accept probability is bounded near 1e-6, yielding 0 observed errors at τ=0 on HumanEval with 15.6% coverage on LiveCodeBench. SEP (arXiv:2604.06485) partitions by symbolic execution into bounded equivalence classes; DiffCodeGen (arXiv:2605.20473) uses coverage-guided fuzzing to synthesize distinguishing inputs with no pre-existing tests; S* (EMNLP Findings 2025) adds adaptive input synthesis plus an LLM judge on divergent outputs; MIST-RL (arXiv:2603.01409) trains test generators by marginal mutation utility and reranks with a candidate×suite vote-count matrix.
findings.open_corner: Every located selector treats each test as an EQUAL, BINARY, INFALLIBLE vote. CodeT counts tests passed; MIST-RL maximizes total votes over suites; Functional Clustering treats the suite as a fixed partition oracle and explicitly concedes it only models the miss probability as (1−δ)^m without ever estimating δ or adapting; SEP uses public examples merely as a 'lightweight validity' pre-filter. No located inference-time method assigns test j a signed reliability pair (sensitivity, specificity) and aggregates a weighted posterior. The sharpest untouched sub-case is the FALSE-POSITIVE test — a wrong generated test that fails correct code. CodeT measures 'test case toxicity rate' as a descriptive statistic only; R2E-Gym (arXiv:2504.07164) names test toxicity and low distinguishability as the failure modes of execution-based verifiers but responds with a two-stage pipeline (execution filter, then learned execution-free reranker) rather than a joint model, so a toxic test still hard-kills a correct patch before reranking ever sees it. Falsifiable claim: on HumanEval+/MBPP+/BigCodeBench, an aggregator that lets a candidate survive failing a test the model infers to be toxic — because that test's failure pattern across candidates is anomalous relative to its estimated specificity — recovers items that CodeT and any filter-then-rerank pipeline structurally cannot recover, and does so specifically on the decisive stratum where the pass-count plurality is wrong.

findings.area: Explicit measurement of verification STRENGTH (mutation score, detection rate, suite adequacy) and where that number is allowed to go
findings.what_is_solved: Verification strength is measured well and the numbers are damning, which is the empirical foundation the lens needs. EvalPlus (arXiv:2305.01210) showed 80x test augmentation drops pass@k by 19.3-28.9% and reorders model rankings, and that 11% of HumanEval ground-truth solutions were themselves wrong. SAGA/TCGBench (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2507.06920) proposes multi-dimensional test-suite thoroughness metrics including detection rate (90.62%) and 'verifier accuracy' (32.58%, +10.78 points over LiveCodeBench-v6). STING (arXiv:2604.01518) mutation-diagnoses SWE-bench Verified and finds 77% of instances admit at least one semantically-wrong surviving variant that passes the gold suite; augmenting the suites drops top-10 repair agents' resolved rates by 4.2-9.0%. Independently, 29.6% of 'plausible' SWE-bench Verified patches are behaviorally incorrect. VeRPO (arXiv:2601.03525) is the closest anyone comes to using strength as a weight: it computes each unit test's empirical pass rate ρ_j over a rollout group and forms w'_j = exp(−α·ρ_j)/(N̂(ρ_j)+δ) with a KDE density correction.
findings.open_corner: Measured strength is used exclusively to BUILD better suites (SAGA, MIST-RL, MuTAP, Meta's ACH) or to RE-BENCHMARK agents (EvalPlus, STING), never as a parameter inside an inference-time decision rule. VeRPO is the sole weighting case and is disqualified on three axes it states itself: the weight is batch-global (all solutions in a batch share identical test weights), it applies exclusively to the RL policy-gradient reward and is never used for inference-time candidate selection, and it assumes tests are reliable with no false-positive or flakiness term. The open corner: mutation kill rate is a per-test property computable at inference time with ZERO labels — mutate the candidate program, check whether test j still fails it — yet no located work uses candidate-conditional mutation discrimination as the reliability prior for test j's verdict on that specific candidate. That closes the loop STING opens: STING proves 77% of gold suites are under-constrained but then only regenerates tests; it never converts 'this suite is weak here' into 'therefore discount this pass'. Falsifiable claim: a per-(test, candidate) strength score derived from local mutation kill, used as the precision parameter of that verdict in a weighted posterior, outperforms both raw pass-count and VeRPO-style global difficulty weights on decisive-stratum selection accuracy at matched execution budget.

findings.area: Budget allocation and value-of-information across a heterogeneous menu of weak checks

Adaptive Generate-Rank-Verify (Dughmi, Haghifam, Kalayci, arXiv:2605.17609) sets up inference-time search where a ranker orders candidates and a budget of verification queries is adaptively allocated, with formal analysis of when to concentrate budget, evaluated on HMMT and Qwen2.5-Coder code reasoning. SARA (arXiv:2607.26253) casts per-step rollout collection as budget-constrained optimal stopping, exploiting that a group's effectiveness is decided within its first few rollouts. findings.open_corner: Adaptive GRV models verification as a PERFECT-but-costly oracle with a SINGLE mechanism at UNIFORM cost per query, and its own future-work section names precisely the three gaps: extension to probabilistic/noisy verification oracles with partial correctness signals, heterogeneous verifier costs, and multiple verification sources. No located work computes expected information gain per unit wall-clock cost across a genuinely heterogeneous check menu whose costs span four orders of magnitude — type check (~ms), single generated unit test (~100ms), property-based test with shrinking (~seconds), full mutation-guided suite (~minutes) — conditional on the current posterior over which candidate is correct. That is the exact quantity that dissolves the map's budget wall: in the label-free QA regime any sample diverted from iid voting was a pure loss because no per-sample signal existed, but here a 1ms type check that eliminates 30% of the candidate set has computable positive VoI against the marginal iid sample. Falsifiable claim: on LiveCodeBench/BigCodeBench at fixed total wall-clock, a VoI-greedy scheduler over the check menu beats both (a) uniform 'run the whole suite on everything' and (b) pure iid sampling with terminal majority voting, and the crossover budget at which diverting from sampling starts paying is predictable in advance from estimated check specificities.

findings.area: Partial verification outside code: math substitution/symbolic checks, property-based tests, metamorphic relations, static/type checks
findings.what_is_solved: The individual weak checks exist and work as gates. PROVE (arXiv:2410.12608) translates each NL math solution into a Python program, executes it, discards solutions whose program output disagrees, then majority-votes the survivors — beating vanilla self-consistency zero-shot with no finetuning. CoSineVerifier (arXiv:2512.01224) is a tool-augmented verifier with a Python interpreter and unit-conversion utility, RL-trained to raise tool-invocation accuracy 76%→90%, reaching 91.9% on VerifyBench-Hard. Property-Generated Solver (arXiv:2506.18315) shows LLMs are far better at stating correctness invariants than writing correct code (48.9% validation accuracy vs 1.1% direct generation on hard tasks), and PBT-Bench (arXiv:2605.15229) benchmarks agents on property-based testing. findings.open_corner: Every located non-code partial verifier is a BINARY GATE consumed in isolation. PROVE hard-filters and throws the discarded solution away — a program that disagrees contributes zero graded evidence, and PROVE never estimates how often its own translation step is the thing that is wrong. CoSineVerifier emits [Correct]/[Incorrect] with no confidence and aggregates no multiple weak checks. Daikon-derived invariants are known to be unsound with a high false-positive rate that is currently handled by manual filtering, not by a reliability parameter. No located work aggregates a VECTOR of cheap math checks of manifestly different strength — back-substitution into the original relation, dimensional/unit consistency, numeric evaluation at random sample points, special-case and limit behavior, monotonicity/sign checks, symbolic simplification — into a single calibrated posterior with per-check-type sensitivity and specificity. These check types have stable, estimable reliability profiles across a benchmark (back-substitution is near-perfectly specific but only applies to algebraic forms; numeric spot-checks are high-sensitivity low-specificity), which makes their confusion structure identifiable from a modest calibration set and then reusable label-free. findings.area: Instrument validity of executable verifiers on the decisive stratum (where the plurality is wrong)
findings.what_is_solved: That verifier reliability is difficulty-dependent rather than constant is now established for LM verifiers. 'Variation in Verification' (arXiv:2509.17995) decomposes verification into TPR (accept-correct) and TNR (reject-incorrect) and finds TPR rises steadily as problems get easier while TNR shows no clean difficulty relation; crucially, as GENERATORS get stronger TNR drops substantially while TPR barely moves — stronger generators produce harder-to-detect errors. It reports TPR saturation near 0.65 on hard math, and finds verifier-capability correlation is linear (r>0.9) only at medium difficulty with threshold effects at the extremes. Weaver's Appendix B.4 independently observes that weak verifiers are highly accurate on easy queries and poor on hard ones, and tries per-difficulty-cluster weak-supervision models as a partial fix.
findings.open_corner: 'Variation in Verification' covers math, MMLU-Pro, and NL reasoning across 4,400+ problems with NO code execution and no executable environments — the paper's own scope excludes exactly the cheap-truth regime — and it stratifies by difficulty quartile without ever restricting to the stratum where majority voting actually fails. Weaver's difficulty clustering keys off the empirical correct-to-incorrect ratio, which is a label-dependent proxy, and still fits a verifier-level (not item-level) model. So the instrument-validity split — overall signal quality versus signal quality specifically on plurality-wrong items — has never been measured for ANY executable verifier. Nobody has published, for generated unit tests, property checks, type checks, or SWE-bench reproduction tests, the pair (sensitivity, specificity) CONDITIONAL on the item being one where the label-free plurality is wrong. This matters because the map's whole negative result was driven by anchors that looked good overall and were dead on the decisive stratum; the entire cheap-truth thesis rests on executable checks NOT degrading the same way, and that is currently an untested assumption. proposal:
# Three Candidates for the Cheap-Truth Program

---

## Candidate 1 — **KAPPA**: Kill-Anchored Per-verdict Precision Assignment

### Mechanism

1. **Standard front end.** N candidates, M generated tests, execute → pass matrix `B ∈ {0,1}^{N×M}`. Cluster candidates by behavioral fingerprint over the test inputs (free, DiffCodeGen/SemanticVote style) → clusters `C_1..C_L`, representatives `r_1..r_L`. Typically L ≈ 5–15 for N = 50.
2. **Neighborhood synthesis (no LLM).** For each representative `r_l`, emit K ≈ 20 AST-level semantic mutants: comparison flips, `<`↔`<=`, off-by-one on indices/loop bounds, branch deletion, early-return removal, return-value perturbation on edge cases. Discard only non-compiling mutants; keep crashers.
3. **Local kill rate.** `κ_lj = (1/K) Σ_k 1[test j fails mutant k of r_l]`. Zero labels, zero LLM calls, zero reference to the tally. Cost: `L·K·M` executions per problem.
4. **Per-verdict likelihood ratio.** Model `P(pass | correct) = 1 − ε_j` and `P(pass | incorrect) = 1 − κ_lj`. Then
   `LLR(pass) = log((1−ε_j)/(1−κ_lj))`, `LLR(fail) = log(ε_j / κ_lj)`, clipped to `[η, 1−η]`, η = 0.02.
   `score_l = Σ_j LLR_lj` (pre-register both with and without a `log|C_l|` prior, to test whether the tally is needed at all).
5. **Toxicity guard (secondary).** Over the extended program population (candidates ∪ mutants ≈ N + L·K programs), build a conflict graph: edge `(j,k)` if no program in the population passes both `t_j` and `t_k`. High-conflict tests get `ε_j` inflated. This is the only component that touches assertion-correctness rather than assertion-tightness.

**The central assumption, stated plainly:** the mutant population is a usable proxy for the distribution of *nearby wrong programs*. `κ_lj` is therefore an estimate of test j's specificity localized at cluster l. This is directly checkable post hoc (compare `κ_lj` against the true `P(fail | incorrect)` computed over actual incorrect candidates with hidden labels) and costs nothing extra.

### Assets exploited
TACT signed reliability (κ supplies the specificity term per verdict; because it is per-(test, cluster), it can represent a test that is *tight around the wrong cluster and vacuous around the right one* — a shape no per-test scalar weight can express). Instrument-validity split. Decisive-stratum protocol.

### Delta vs closest prior art
- **ACES** (arXiv:2604.03922): weight is per-test, estimated by LOO-AUC against the tally-induced ranking, then clipped at 0. On the decisive stratum that reference ranking is inverted at the top by definition, so ACES-C zeroes exactly the rescuing tests. κ has **no reference ranking** — it is computed from a program population the tally never enters.
- **B4** (2409.08692): assumes `θ_y` via a Beta prior with `α_y ≫ 1`. KAPPA measures the specificity term instead of priming it.
- **VeRPO** (2601.03525): per-test weight `exp(−α ρ_j)` from batch-global pass rate, RL reward only, no false-positive term, identical weights for all solutions in a batch. KAPPA's weight varies *within* a problem across candidates.
- **Functional Clustering** (2506.11021): models the miss probability as `(1−δ)^m` and concedes it never estimates δ. KAPPA estimates δ per (test, cluster).
- **STING** (2604.01518) / mutation-testing lines: mutation is used to *build better suites* or *re-benchmark agents*. Nobody converts local kill rate into a verdict discount at inference time.
- **CodeT**: `sqrt(|S_x|)·|S_y|` — all tests count equally.

### Pre-registered falsifiers
- **F0 (redundancy).** Regress `κ_lj` on `p_j`, `p_j(1−p_j)`, LOO-AUC, test length. If partial R² > 0.7 **and** decisive-stratum top-1 is within CI of ACES-C, KAPPA is a reparametrization — kill it.
- **F1 (trivial baselines, both required).** Must beat (a) unweighted pass-count plurality, and (b) **the DiffCodeGen medoid — largest behavioral cluster, zero assertions**. Failing (b) means assertions carry no value and weighting them better is pointless; that outcome hands the program to the economics study instead.
- **F2 (matched budget).** Charge every mutation execution. Comparison arms receive the identical wall-clock/token budget as extra candidates and extra tests, at the measured exchange rate.
- **F3 (instrument validity).** Report `δ̄_overall` and `δ̄_decisive` for raw and κ-weighted verdicts. Prediction: raw `δ̄_decisive ≤ 0.05`, κ-weighted `δ̄_decisive ≥ 0.15`. If κ-weighting does not move `δ̄_decisive`, the design is dead regardless of end-task numbers.
- **F4 (mechanism attribution).** Partition decisive items into **vacuity-driven** (every test the wrong plurality passes has low κ around it) vs **toxicity-driven** (a high-κ test asserts the wrong thing and the correct candidate fails it). Prediction: vacuity ≥ 50%. If toxicity ≥ 70%, KAPPA's core cannot help and only the conflict graph matters — report as negative and pivot.
- **F5.** HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench (recent, contamination-controlled window), BigCodeBench. Per-benchmark reporting, no pooling.

### Cheapest decisive test
**Phase 0 builds no algorithm.** One capable open-weights model, HumanEval+ (164) + MBPP+ (378), N = 50, M = 100. Compute hidden labels, identify the decisive stratum, then run **only F3 + F4 + F1(b)**. That yields the instrument-validity split for the executable channel and the vacuity/toxicity decomposition — both currently unpublished — and decides whether the rest gets built.
Cost: ~13.5M output tokens for candidates, ~11M for tests (~$150–400 self-hosted or mid-tier API); ~2.7M candidate×test executions plus ~11M mutant executions at ~5 ms, 64-way parallel ≈ 12–24 h on one 64-core box. **Under $500, under one week including engineering.**

## Candidate 2 — **LEDGER**: Label-free E-process Decision for Execution Rationing

### Mechanism

1. **Priced check menu**, costs measured not assumed: compile/type check (~1–10 ms), public example (~50 ms), single generated unit test (~50–300 ms), differential execution on a fuzzer input (~ms, batched), property test with shrinking (~1–10 s), mutation-guided sweep (~minutes).
2. State = partially observed verdict tensor (candidates × checks) with unpaid cells.
3. **Exchangeability by construction.** Randomize the *reveal order* of cells within each check family, then apply sampling-without-replacement empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences (Waudby-Smith/Ramdas) to each candidate's score over the finite check pool. Validity requires no assumption about how the tests were generated — you are betting on your own randomization, not on the LLM's.
4. **Futility certificate.** Stop when, with probability ≥ 1−α, no assignment of unrevealed cells consistent with the current confidence sequences lets any non-incumbent overtake the incumbent. **Honest estimand: this certifies the search is over, not that the answer is right.**
5. **Divert-or-sample decision.** Extend with an e-process bound on the probability that a fresh candidate lands outside all observed behavioral clusters (Good–Turing style), turning the generate-vs-verify split from grid search into a certified decision.
6. **VoI-greedy scheduling** between certificates: next cell maximizes expected futility-gap reduction per measured unit cost.

### Assets exploited
Betting/e-process fluency — the survey confirms this confluence is empty. Instrument-validity split used to *choose an honest estimand* rather than to certify correctness. Decisive-stratum protocol used to test coverage stability, which a certificate over an observable should have by construction — that claim is testable and is the one thing none of the six dead designs possessed.

### Delta vs closest prior art
- **BEACON** (2510.15945): Bayesian-optimal stopping under conjugate reward-model posteriors; no execution, no anytime validity, coverage collapses under misspecification.
- **CITE** (2605.05873): anytime-valid certification of the *mode of the sampling distribution*, explicitly excluding execution. Different estimand; no cost heterogeneity.
- **ADAP / Adaptive GRV** (2605.17609): perfect oracle, uniform cost, monotonicity assumption — which is precisely what fails when the test channel shares the generator's error modes. LEDGER needs no monotonicity because it certifies the observable. ADAP's own stated future work names noisy oracles, heterogeneous costs, and multiple sources — this is that paper, which is an honest but **novelty-capped** position.
- **SemanticVote / DiffCodeGen**: no stopping rule at all.

### Pre-registered falsifiers
- **F0 (trivial baselines).** "Run everything on everything," and "stop at the first candidate passing all public examples." Must beat the second on accuracy and the first on cost within a pre-registered non-inferiority margin (Δ ≤ 0.5 pp).
- **F1 (matched budget — the likely killer).** At LEDGER's actual wall clock, give plain iid sampling + plurality the same wall clock as extra candidates. If it matches, the certificate bought nothing. This is the budget wall transplanted verbatim.
- **F2 (coverage, stratified).** Empirical miscoverage ≤ α on both overall and decisive strata, α = 0.1. A certificate valid overall and anti-conservative on decisive items reproduces the program's known failure mode and kills the design.
- **F3.** Savings must exceed measured scheduler overhead.
- **F4.** LiveCodeBench + BigCodeBench, N ∈ {10, 100}, no pooling.

### Cheapest decisive test
LEDGER's decisive property: **the tensor is collected once and every policy is then simulated for free by replaying reveals from cache.** LiveCodeBench recent 200 problems, N = 50, full menu. Collection ≈ Candidate 1's Phase 0 (~$200–400, ~1 day compute); policy comparison (LEDGER vs BEACON vs fixed-n vs run-everything vs iid-plurality) costs nothing. **Under $500, and lower marginal cost per hypothesis tested than any other candidate here.**

## Candidate 3 — **REGCAL**: The Repo's Own Suite as a Model-Independent Calibration Pool

### Mechanism
1. SWE-bench-lite/Verified; k ≈ 10 patches per issue (use released trajectory patch sets where possible to avoid generation cost).
2. Build `R`, the model-independent verdict matrix: the repo's **pre-existing human-written tests**, coverage-filtered to those touching the patch's changed lines (raises variance), plus STING-style mutants derived from the *repo*, not the model.
3. Fingerprint and cluster patches over `R`.
4. **Per-issue signed reliability of the generated reproduction test g:** `δ̂ = P(g passes | R-latent correct) − P(g passes | R-latent incorrect)`. Independence claim: `R`'s columns were authored by humans before the model existed, so their errors cannot be correlated with the model's misreading of the issue text. The reference is not the tally.
5. Route: `δ̂ > τ` → g selects; `δ̂ ≈ 0` → fall back to R-clustering; `δ̂ < −τ` → **invert** and prefer patches that fail g. Nobody has assigned a negative weight to a test verdict.

### Assets exploited
TACT signed reliability — this is the only setting in the program where inversion is estimable from a genuinely independent reference. Instrument-validity split. Decisive-stratum protocol adapted to (issue, patch pool).

### Delta vs closest prior art
Issue2Test / EvoOtter / Echo *improve* the reproduction test. UTBoost / STING *strengthen suites for evaluation*. ORACLE-SWE *ranks* oracle signals in aggregate (Reproduction Test ≫ … ≫ Regression Test). R2E-Gym filters then reranks, so a toxic test hard-kills a correct patch before reranking sees it. **No located work uses the existing regression suite as a calibration pool to estimate the signed reliability of the generated reproduction test**, and no work estimates per-issue signed reliability in the single-test regime where ACES/B4/BACE are all inapplicable.

### Pre-registered falsifiers
- **F0 (gating pre-test — cheapest item in this document).** Measure per-issue entropy of `R` across sampled patches. Proceed only if, after coverage filtering and mutation strengthening, median per-issue column entropy > 0.1 bits on ≥ 40% of issues. If plausible patches pass everything, the calibration pool is degenerate and the design dies before it is built.
- **F1 (trivial baselines).** Majority patch by R-fingerprint; and "always trust g" (current practice).
- **F2 (matched budget).** Charge mutation strengthening and extra suite runs; comparison arm gets equal dollars as more sampled patches.
- **F3 (the risky prediction).** On the decisive stratum, `δ̂_decisive ≤ 0` — the reproduction test is anti-informative exactly where it decides, because a test written from the same issue text inherits the misreading that produced the wrong patch. If `δ̂_decisive > 0.2`, the premise is wrong and the honest result is "reproduction tests are fine."
- **F4 (power).** ≥ 15% of issues must be decisive at k = 10, or the study is underpowered and must not run.

### Cheapest decisive test
F0 alone: ~300 issues × 5 patches × one coverage-filtered suite run ≈ 25–250 core-hours, **$50–200, one week** (Docker harness engineering dominates). Full study: 3000 patch evaluations at 1–10 min each ≈ **$1–3k and roughly a month**.

# Ranking

Scored as (expected novelty) × P(survives adversarial review), where "survives" means it does not die of the shape that killed the previous six designs: *estimator references the tally; signal is per-item not per-sample; estimand is correctness but the instrument identifies only agreement; diverted budget exceeds coverage gained; the 1–2 vote winner is unselectable; errors are stable-wrong.*

**1. KAPPA — 0.85 × 0.50 ≈ 0.42**

The only candidate that severs the tally reference at the mechanism level rather than the estimand level. `κ` is computed from a program population the tally never touches, it is per-verdict rather than per-item, and because evidence weight is decoupled from vote count it is the only design here that attacks the **cashing wall** directly: a single correct candidate can win on high-κ passes.

Brutal case against: `κ` measures *tightness*, not *truthfulness*. A toxic test that encodes the model's shared misconception can be locally tight and still assert the wrong thing — and if the decisive stratum is toxicity-dominated, KAPPA's core is inert and only the conflict-graph bolt-on remains, which is the weakest, least-proven part. Second, if `κ` turns out to be mostly `p_j(1−p_j)` in disguise, this is ACES with extra compute. Third and most dangerous: SemanticVote found all aggregation rules statistically indistinguishable across 18 configurations and DiffCodeGen matched them at 4% of the token cost with **no assertions at all**. If the assertion channel is worthless, weighting it better is worthless. That is why the DiffCodeGen medoid is a *required* Phase-0 baseline, not an optional one.

**2. LEDGER — 0.55 × 0.80 ≈ 0.44**

Nominally the higher product and within noise of KAPPA. Highest survival probability of anything here, because it wins by refusing to certify correctness: the randomized-reveal construction makes the martingale valid without any assumption about how the tests were generated, and the estimand — "further execution cannot change the choice" — is one the executable channel genuinely identifies. It cannot die of two-world unidentifiability because it never claims to resolve the two worlds.

Brutal case against: it wins money, not accuracy, and the map already says the accuracy window is thin. Its most likely obituary is "correct, rigorous, and ignored" — the second-most-likely being F1, where matched-wall-clock iid sampling with plurality simply equals it and the certificate is revealed as overhead. It also answers, almost line for line, the stated future work of a 2026 paper (ADAP), which caps its novelty ceiling regardless of execution quality. And it does nothing for the cashing wall or for stable-wrong.

**Tiebreaker, declared explicitly as outside the stated metric:** KAPPA leads because its Phase 0 is a *publishable measurement under total mechanism failure* — the executable-channel instrument-validity split (`δ̄_overall` vs `δ̄_decisive`) and the vacuity/toxicity decomposition of the decisive stratum are both unpublished and both settle whether the cheap-truth thesis holds at its root. LEDGER's failure mode produces a null with no accompanying finding. Run LEDGER's tensor collection **on the same data collection as KAPPA Phase 0** — the menus overlap almost entirely, so the marginal cost of carrying both to the decision point is a few hundred dollars, and one collection buys two independent decisions.

**3. REGCAL — 0.80 × 0.35 ≈ 0.28**

Highest single-claim novelty in the set — the independence argument (human-written, pre-existing, model-independent verdict columns) is the cleanest circularity break available anywhere in this survey, and it lands precisely where the survey says the whole signed-reliability toolkit is inapplicable.

Brutal case against: it is one empirical fact away from being dead, and that fact is unfavorable by default. On SWE-bench, nearly all plausible patches pass the existing suite — `R` is very likely all ones, which makes the calibration pool degenerate and the entire method undefined. Coverage filtering and mutation strengthening are the proposed rescues, and STING's own 77%-surviving-variants result is simultaneously the argument that they *can* work and the evidence that the base suite is far too weak. It is also 3–6× the cost of the others, with heavy per-repo containerization engineering, and the decisive stratum may be too small at k = 10 to power anything.

**Recommendation:** run F0 of REGCAL ($50–200, one week) *concurrently* with KAPPA Phase 0, since it is nearly free and gates a month of work. Fund KAPPA Phase 0 as the primary; collect LEDGER's tensor from the same runs. Three decisions, one data collection, under $1,000 total, roughly three weeks.
